_raw.title: Evan Smith Joins Zero Skateboards Following the Closure of His Own Brand Umaverse
_raw.text:
Professional skateboarders starting their own companies has become a common part of the skateboarding industry.

Some manage to build a lasting business, while others eventually decide to step away and find a new home with an established company.

As we previously reported, professional skateboarder Evan Smith has officially closed his own skateboard brand, Umaverse, formerly known as UMA Landsled.

READ MORE: Pro Skateboarder Evan Smith’s Umaverse Skateboard Brand Shuts Down

After spending nearly two years as a free agent, Smith has finally landed a new home with Jamie "The Chief" Thomas and Zero Skateboards.

The announcement gives core heads a look at what's next for the Pennsylvania born skateboarder, who has spent years building his reputation through his creative street skating.

The news came shortly after Zero released its latest video, After Forever, featuring some of the team's riders.

Along with the video release came the announcement that Smith is now officially part of the Zero squad.

RELATED: Uma Landsleds Receives Cease & Desist From Puma, Rebrands as Umaverse

Zero shared a few clips from the new video on social media, giving skaters a preview of Smith's skating while confirming that his full part and first board release are on the way.

Zero Skateboards posted:

"@starheadbody is on ZERO!!
Here are a few clips from our new video ‘After Forever’ now playing on the @thrashermag site. Full Evan part & board release coming soon! 💀"

It's great to see Smith back with a skateboard company, especially one with the history and reputation of Zero.

Now we're looking forward to seeing what kind of graphics he comes up with and, of course, getting our first look at his full part in After Forever.

A post shared by Zero Skateboards (@zeroskateboards)

_raw.title: WHY IS THIS FURRY SKATE VIDEO SO DAMN GOOD?
_raw.text:
WHY IS THIS FURRY SKATE VIDEO SO DAMN GOOD?

November 10, 2026/
        Ben Komins/        ARTICLES, VIDEOS/
                Comments: 1

“I built this algorithm brick by brick.”

That’s the triumphant thought that ran through my head when I came across Scruff, a furry skate vid, while scrolling YouTube.

For those less online, a furry is someone who likes to dress up as cartoonish animal characters. It’s a heavily meme-ified, smirk-worthy subculture, and thanks to Scruff, it’s now a part of skateboarding.

The video’s colorful, rave-like editing style, bubblegum bass soundtrack, and abundance of swinging tails make it unlike anything else I’ve seen. And since watching, I have brought up the video to anyone who will listen.

And wouldn’t you know, people love it. It’s bold and unflinching. If it were a summer stunt, it would be a cannonball into the deep end. I had to know, in a skate world that breeds cool-guy insecurity and copycats, how’d this crew of furries find each other?

After poking around, I found Santos Probst, the editor of and second skater in the video. At just 20-years-old, they were quick to open up about how the video came together, and in a series of surprises, it ended up being one of my favorite conversations of the year.

You know, I genuinely haven’t seen a comment section that positive in a while.
It’s insane. There’s a lot of comments from politically right-leaning people or people commenting like, “I’m an old head and I thought I would hate this, but actually loved it.” I don’t know if you’ve seen this one, but there’s this amazing Twitter comment where someone’s like, “Still voting red, but good video” [laughs].

I wanted to make something that wasn’t afraid to scare the normies, but ironically, I feel like that was so refreshing to people that it got less hate than any random given skate video. It’s not like the video did insanely well, but I was expecting it to get 2K views. I was like, “This is going to be really important to 20 gay furries who live in San Francisco.”

“I wanted to make a video where we were the weird thing happening, and it was presented as straightforward and not insecure or ironic as possible.”

Do you think that because you really went for it, that’s kind of why it hit?
I just wanted to make something that was maximalist, but I feel like everything in skating right now that’s maximalist is super ironic or insecure, and then everything that’s not maximalist and traditional is really self-congratulatory.

Skaters have this way of, and I think this is a Strobeck thing, but they’ll film something weird happening on the street and then put it in their video, and it’s looking down on it like, “Oh, look how weird this weird thing is.”But I look at that and I’m like, “You aren’t better than any of those people.” Skaters have a hard time being the butt of the joke, and I wanted to make a video where we were the weird thing happening, and it was presented as straightforward and not insecure or ironic as possible.

How did the Scruff crew originally come about?
Scruff came about out of convenience. I’m a furry and a skateboarder and all my friends are furries and skateboarders and we don’t live very close to each other, so we would meet up at furry conventions. If you go to a furry convention, you’ll meet three new people who you’ve never met before who skate. If you throw down, someone will hear the wheels and come rolling by or something.

Scruff was going to happen no matter what. It’s crazy seeing how many furry skaters there are, and no one was making videos really showing the intersection of the cultures.

So the skaters in this video found each other through going to these furry conventions?
Some of us did, but me, Nicole and Space all met in the Gifted Hater Discord server. We’re all straight out of that ilk, that generation of skaters. There’s a lot of lore, but we’re like Gifted Hater’s children, basically internet babies. All of the Scruff stuff now is in an offshoot Discord s

_raw.title: LA CASITA DIY – Málaga, Spain – HALLOWEEN 2026
_raw.text:
Words and photos: Letícia Nogueira

It’s been 10 years of La Casita, this magical DIY in the South of Spain, and we got word this year that the place is going to be demolished soon. It’s not very tough of me to say that I cried my eyes out when I got the news, but overall there’s a stoic feeling in the air, as the lads keep throwing the ole saying around in nonchalance: everything comes to an end.

There’s always a Halloween party at La Casita, but this one was going to be the last, so a bunch of DIY freaks gathered there to celebrate and bid farewell. From Andalusia to the Basque Country, Catalonia and Murcia, the place was full of DIY legends from Spain. The destruction party was on! It was hectic. It was a blast. It was epic.

From Andalusia to the Basque Country, Catalonia and Murcia, the place was full of DIY legends from Spain. The destruction party was on! It was hectic. It was a blast. It was epic.

Even the police came to check out the party; and kicked everyone out. It was intense! They threatened to put us all in jail if we didn’t evacuate the place. After 45 minutes of trying to put some sense into them, they went back on their word and told us to get back to it. There were tears, there were cheers; it was a rollercoaster of emotions. The party went on, fireworks, illegal shenanigans and all, and it was wholesome as fuck to be all there together.

Everyone absolutely destroyed the whole DIY. The pool sessions were rad. The gigs were sick. We had Emuna with their death metal, Tricoderma and My State with their punk rock, all the freaks dancing the night away. At the end of the night, skater duo from Seville Acid Drop played their instrumental doom and roll that had us all delighted as if we’d just tasted the cherry on top of the cake.

But the most awaited event of the night was The Skateboard Inquisitors’ performace, which was more like a satanic ritual; a ceremony to the slash grind and the Don’t-Fucking-Do-It attitude. An homage to hostile terrain and radical coping, they played their number one hit “Fuck Normal Coping, Fuck Normal People” and, together with the crowd, they literally destroyed the most humble metal coping in La Casita, which everyone agreed to being gross anyway.

The next day, that ramp was completely destroyed. Everyone was hungover, except for the ones who didn’t even sleep. Some people woke up with new tattoos they didn’t even remember getting. Billy Slasher paid a visit to the hospital overnight, got emergency surgery and was back by morning to finish his bottle of Jack Daniels. Many of the lads went back home with injuries, even the ones who didn’t skate. It was perfect.

_raw.title: Nachwuchschallenge 2026
_raw.text:
Die Nachwuchschallenge ist eine Sichtungsmaßnahme der Sportkommission Skateboard im DRIV e.V. für junge Skateboarder*innen im Alter von 7 bis 10 Jahren. Anders als bei einem klassischen Contest absolvieren die Teilnehmenden acht Stationen im Challenge-Format. Dabei zeigen sie ihre sportmotorischen Grundlagen wie Balancieren und Springen sowie ihr Trickrepertoire in den Kategorien Flat, Grind & Slide und Transition.

Im Mittelpunkt stehen nicht nur die aktuellen Leistungen, sondern auch die individuellen Stärken und Entwicklungspotenziale. Die Challenge bietet die Möglichkeit, Erfahrungen zu sammeln und neue Impulse für die sportliche Entwicklung mitzunehmen. Bei sehr guten Ergebnissen können sich zudem Perspektiven für eine Aufnahme in den Regional- oder Landeskader ergeben.

Die Nachwuchschallenge ist zugleich Bestandteil der bundesweiten Nachwuchsleistungsbewertung.

Auf Grundlage der Rahmenrichtlinie (RRL) des DOSB werden die Ergebnisse der Altersklasse 1 (AK1) bundesweit vergleichbar bewertet. Daraus entstehen Bewertungspunkte, die eine Grundlage für Förderentscheidungen der Landessportbünde bilden.

In der Altersklasse 2 (11–14 Jahre) erfolgt die Bewertung über nationale, in der Altersklasse 3 (14–18 Jahre) über internationale Kriteriumswettkämpfe.

Standorte der Nachwuchschallenge 2026:

* West: Köln (HE, NRW, RP, SL)

* Süd: Stuttgart, Karlsruhe, München (BY, BW)

* Nord: Hamburg (HB, HH, NI)

* Mitte: Leipzig (SN, ST, TH)

* Nord-Ost: Berlin, Cottbus (BE, BB, MV)

Anmeldung und weitere Informationen: www.nachwuchschallenge.de

Ginwoo Onodera, 16, and Yumeka Oda won the 2026 Street World Championship in Paraguay. Full results, and a men's final where the first Best Trick landing came after twelve straight misses.

This report uses World Skate's event reports and the official result lists for every round. Where a detail comes from one source only, we say so. The graphics are ours, because official event photos are not free to reuse.

The total is best run plus best trick, out of a maximum of 200. In the men's final only three skaters landed a Best Trick at all (Nagai, Kang, Onodera). In the women's final seven started, and between them they landed nine.

The course and the format

The course at the Paraguayan Olympic Committee campus was a full rebuild by Rio Ramp Design and California Skateparks. It has a nine-stair handrail, very long flat bars, a kicker over stairs and chunky A-frame rails. The aim, according to World Skate's Luca Basilico, was a course that countries building skateparks today can copy.

The road to the final

The men's final: the Best Trick curse

After the run section, Giovanni Vianna, Angelo Caro, Ivan Monteiro, Netsuke and defending champion Sasaki were all in the mix. Then the Best Trick section began, and nobody landed anything. World Skate counted twelve failed attempts in a row.

Nagai breaks the streak. On his second attempt, Taiga Nagai landed a Bigspin Front Blunt Shove-It on the handrail for 83.09. It was enough for bronze, more than 80 points clear of fourth place, because no one else landed a trick.

Kang's fall and comeback. Kang Juni caught his toe on the hubba and landed on his face. The medics called for a stretcher, but he got up, had his wrist taped and came back. On his second attempt he landed a Switch 270 Lipslide over the gap to rail for 90.11.

Onodera's last attempt. Onodera had run 90.14 and needed a trick worth more than 89. He missed his second attempt, then landed a Bigflip Front Blunt Bigspin out on his third for 92.12. Total 182.26 against Kang's 179.32, a margin of 2.94 points.

It was Onodera's first World Skateboarding Tour win. Wikipedia lists him as born in 2010, so he is 16. For Kang, 18 according to SBS, the silver is the best result South Korean skateboarding has had at a World Championship, one month after Korea's first Asian Games skateboarding gold.

The women's final: Oda over Covell

Wilton withdrew through illness, so seven women started. They landed nine Best Tricks, three times as many as the men.

This is Oda's second world title. Wikipedia lists her birth date as 30 October 2006, so she is 19.

Where the sources disagree

World Skate calls the event the first big points event on the Road to LA28. The ranking points are not published in the sources we could read, so we cannot say how many Onodera, Kang, Oda and Covell earned.

Surf Forecasts Like a Pro: Buoys, Best Sites and Where to Check the Waves

How forecasters read ocean buoys, which surf forecast sites are free and which are worth paying for, which tools suit which coast, plus webcam and surf spot sites. With prices, sources and a list of what we could not verify.

Dieser Artikel ist derzeit nur auf Englisch verfügbar.

Every surf forecast starts in the same place: a storm somewhere far out at sea. Wind blows over a stretch of water, builds waves, and those waves travel for days until they reach a coast. A forecast is a computer model's guess about that journey. A buoy is a measurement of what actually arrived at one point.

Professional forecasters use both. They run the model, then check it against the buoys. This guide explains how that works, so you can do the same, and then lists the free and paid sites, which ones suit which coast, where to find webcams, and where to look up surf spots.

One note on how we wrote this. "Best" in surf forecasting is partly a matter of taste and partly a matter of where you surf, and nobody has run a head-to-head accuracy test of every site on every coast. Where we recommend something, we say what the recommendation rests on. Where we could not confirm a detail, we say that too, and the last section collects those gaps. Prices are as published when we checked, in October 2026, and they change.

How a forecast is made

Forecasters need a few ingredients: wind speed, how long the wind blows, and the distance it blows over, called the fetch. Wikipedia's article on surf forecasting lists swell height, direction and period, plus the shape of the sea floor, tides and local weather, as what turns offshore swell data into an estimate for a beach. It also says plainly that an exact prediction of the surf is impossible, but a good estimate is not.

Two kinds of swell are worth telling apart. Groundswell is generated far offshore, has a long period and usually makes better surf. Wind swell is made by local winds, has a short period and is smaller and choppier.

The computer models do the heavy lifting, but they drift from reality. The fix is to feed in buoy measurements. Sofar Ocean, which runs a network of small wave buoys, describes the idea simply: when a buoy's measurement differs from the model's value, the model's starting estimate is adjusted toward the observation, and that corrected state becomes the start of the forecast. Sofar says it has done this with its buoys' wave heights since December 2019.

The same logic works for you. The University Corporation for Atmospheric Research teaches forecasters to check whether a model started from the right place by comparing it with buoy observations. If the buoy shows 2 m at 14 seconds and your forecast site claims 1 m at 9 seconds, the forecast is wrong, and you will know before you drive to the beach.

How the pros read a buoy

A caution first. We found plenty of documentation on how professional forecasters and researchers use buoys. We did not find a source describing what individual pro surfers do day to day, so we do not claim to. What follows is the method forecasters publish and teach.

1. Wave height is not the biggest wave. Significant wave height is the average of the biggest third of waves. Sofar notes that the biggest single wave is about twice that, so a 3 m reading means some waves near 6 m. Stormsurf's buoy FAQ says the same about once an hour.

2. Period matters more than height. The period is the time between wave crests. Stormsurf puts it bluntly: small amounts of long-period energy are far more rideable and powerful than larger quantities of short-period energy. Look for energy spikes at periods above 10 seconds.

3. Direction decides whether the swell reaches you. Stormsurf warns that swells passing a buoy are not necessarily heading toward the nearest beach, and that islands, points and wrapping reduce swell size.

Mizuho Hasegawa and Egoitz Bijueska won the 2026 Park World Championship in Paraguay after a week of rain delays, slams and a men's semifinal that took two days to finish. How it unfolded, who made the podium, and what it means for LA28.

Skateboarding competitions are usually decided by who lands their run. In Asunción, Paraguay, the 2026 Park World Championship was decided by who could keep landing runs through rain, injuries and a schedule that kept falling apart. Japan's Mizuho Hasegawa took the women's title and Spain's Egoitz Bijueska took the men's, and both are only 15 years old.

This report is built from World Skate's own event reports, which were sent as newsletters during the week, and checked against independent coverage of the results. Where a detail comes from only one source, we say so. Photos are not included here because the official event photos are distributed to media under World Skate's own terms, so the graphics below are ours.

The podium scores come from the wire report by the Spanish news agency EFE, as carried by Infobae and ABC Color, and the same figures appear in Diario Euskadi's report. Laso's fifth place and 78.83 come from Diario Euskadi and Shredder News. The fourth place in the women's final, and places five to eight in the men's final, are not in the sources we could read, so we leave them out rather than guess. World Skate's own finals report, which we read in full, does not publish scores. It does name the gold medallists, describes Schaar taking second place on his third run ahead of Khury, and says Hasegawa and Brown were the two skaters fighting for first. If you need an official scoresheet, World Skate's results pages are the place to check.

The Park World Championship ran as part of the World Skate Games, which World Skate lists as taking place in Asunción from 3 to 10 October for this event. The park competition was bookended by rain, and both genders had to finish rounds in the morning after the day they started.

World Skate's report describes it as "48 hours of skateboarding action bookended by rain". The women's quarterfinals rolled over into Friday morning. The men's semifinals started on Friday evening in fading light, were stopped by rain with seven runs still to go, and restarted on Saturday morning before the finals.

Women's semifinals: the favourites wobble

The women's semifinals opened with an early sign of how unpredictable the week had been. Japan's Kokona Hiraki, a regular on podiums, started in 15th place and looked relieved just to get a first run in. Spain's Naia Laso landed the Backside 360 over the jumpbox that had beaten her in the quarterfinals.

Heat 2 brought new faces. Chinese Taipei's 14-year-old Yi-Fan "Yvonne" Lin, praised by World Skate for having the best Sugarcane "this side of Chris Miller", opened with a strong first run, and had never before made a World Skateboarding Tour final. California's Minna Stess skated with a composure the Tour had not always seen from her.

Then the heat wobbled. Sky Brown, who had only just qualified out of the quarterfinals that morning, fluffed her opening trick. Finland's Heili Sirvio took a heavy slam. Lillian Erickson, Mizuho Hasegawa and Stess all missed on their next runs, leaving everything open at the halfway point.

It was Sky Brown's second run that put her into finals contention. 2024 World Champion Raicca Ventura then jumped from 13th to 5th, Hasegawa moved up to second, Brown improved again and Ventura answered. In the last run of the day Hasegawa took back top spot. Lin held on in eighth when Sirvio's last run came up short and Erickson slipped out.

_raw.text:
World Skate Games 2026: Mizuho Hasegawa and JD Sanchez Take Vert Gold in Asunción

Japan's Mizuho Hasegawa and the USA's JD Sanchez opened the skateboarding program at the World Skate Games 2026 in Asunción, Paraguay, by winning the women's and men's Vert World Championships — the first titles decided at a Games running through October 18.

Dieser Artikel ist derzeit nur auf Englisch verfügbar.

The first vert skateboarding world titles of the 2026 World Skate Games were handed out this weekend in Asunción, Paraguay — and both went to riders who are becoming very hard to bet against. Japan's Mizuho Hasegawa and the USA's JD Sanchez won the women's and men's Vert World Championships respectively, on a ramp set up in front of Paraguay's presidential palace, as the skateboarding portion of the Games got underway.
Sources: ABC Color (Paraguay), World Skate official event calendar

The Games themselves run October 2–18 in Asunción, bringing together over 10,000 athletes across 12 disciplines, with 154 world titles on the line — including skateboarding's park, street, and slalom events still to come later in the schedule.
Source: Olympics.com

Vert: Skateboarding's Original Discipline

Vert tends to get overshadowed by street skateboarding in terms of mainstream visibility, but it's actually the older of the two — rooted in 1970s pool-riding and the purpose-built ramps that followed, long before street skating became skateboarding's dominant public face in the late 1980s. Two facing transitions, height, and very little room to hide: it's often cited as one of the purest tests in the sport, since there's no flat section to recover on mid-run the way there is in park skating.

Women's Final: Hasegawa Holds Off a Late Push

Hasegawa, already the reigning women's park world champion, entered the vert final with the kind of form that made her the rider to beat. According to coverage from the event, she built an early lead through the run section, only to see Japanese teammate Shuka Kawai close the gap hard in Best Trick — attempting back-to-back 720s in a bid to steal the win outright. Hasegawa answered by stomping a difficult trick of her own on her final attempt to secure the title, with Kawai taking silver. Brazil's Helena Laurino rounded out the podium in third, while 13-year-old Brazilian skater Luiza Hiumi drew attention for an impressively mature opening run in her senior World Championship debut.

Men's Final: Sanchez's Consistency Beats Khury's Power

The men's final came down to a tight contest between Sanchez and Brazil's Gui Khury, a rider already known for pushing the upper limits of vert difficulty. Per event coverage, Khury landed several 900-degree variations during the Best Trick round — including one over an eight-foot channel gap — but Sanchez's broader range of tricks across the full session was enough to edge the win, finishing roughly nine points ahead. Australia's Hudson Walker took bronze. A brief weather delay during the final round of Best Trick had little effect on the minor placings further down the field.

Source: World Skate official results, confirmed after the finals on Saturday, October 3

With the vert titles decided, skateboarding at the Games moves on to park competition (October 3–10) and street (October 11–18), featuring a deep field that includes Olympic medalists Sky Brown and Keegan Palmer among the athletes chasing ranking points toward LA 2028 qualification.
Source: Olympics.com

Flying With a Surfboard: What You Actually Need to Know

Length limits, oversize fees, liability and fin rules for more than fifty airlines, checked against their own pages — plus how to pack a board so it arrives in one piece.

Dieser Artikel ist derzeit nur auf Englisch verfügbar.

A surfboard is the awkward cousin of the skateboard: it's too long for any cabin, it's fragile in exactly the places baggage handlers are rough on, and airlines can't agree on whether it's sports equipment, oversize luggage or something they'd rather not carry at all. The good news is that nearly every major airline will take one. The bad news is that the rules, fees and liability terms differ a lot, and some airlines don't mention surfboards on their official pages at all.

This guide follows the same approach as our skateboard article: every airline rule below is taken from the airline's own wording and linked at the bottom — more than fifty airlines across four regions, with the ones we could not read marked as such. Where we couldn't read an official page — several airline sites block automated readers or hide their fee tables behind JavaScript — we say "not verified" rather than guess. Policies change often, so everything here was checked in October 2026 and should be confirmed with your airline before you book.

A surfboard never goes in the cabin. The four tables below cover the airlines we checked, region by region, with the detail and the gaps in Part 1. The real questions are whether your airline accepts it, how it's priced, and whether it counts inside your normal baggage allowance or as a separate oversize item.

The short version: best and worst deals

Prices cannot be compared like for like across fifty airlines, because most airlines publish a rule rather than a price, and some publish neither. So the ranking below uses only what each airline's own page states. The cheapest airlines are the ones that treat a surfboard as an ordinary checked bag with no surfboard surcharge. The dearest are the ones that add a fixed fee on top, and the chart shows those fees in approximate US dollars.

Best deals. British Airways, Alaska and Hawaiian, KLM, Qantas, Virgin Australia, Air New Zealand, Emirates, Etihad, ANA, Singapore Airlines and Cathay Pacific carry a board inside the normal checked-baggage rules with no separate surfboard fee. Alaska and Hawaiian stand out if you travel with several boards, because a single bag may hold more than one. This only holds if your fare already includes a checked bag.

Most expensive. Thai Airways charges about $150 for a board up to 200 cm and $300 above that on its own flights. Finnair's oversize fee reaches €350 on Europe–Australia, New Zealand and Fiji routes, but only if the board is over 210 cm or 23 kg. Ethiopian ($200) and SriLankan ($250) also look expensive, but both came through a page summary and we could not confirm them. JetBlue charges $150 for oversize and does not accept surfboards on some routes at all.

Cannot be ranked. United, Air France's surf-specific price, Lufthansa, Ryanair and several Latin American airlines state no price we could read. Ask them before you book.

Part 1: Airline policies, region by region

All of these are hold-luggage rules. Each table is read from the airline's own page where we could read it; "not verified" means the page failed to load or did not mention surfboards, not that the airline has no rule. Where an entry came through a page summary rather than a clean read, the notes under the table say so.

What stands out. JetBlue is the only airline whose own contract of carriage bans surfboards on certain routes (Bermuda, Santo Domingo, Santiago in the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Peru and Trinidad and Tobago), so check the destination, not just the airline.
